Sebec Lake adds the camp pattern — bats, squirrels and porcupines in places closed all winter — and the farm roads add groundhogs, skunks and beaver flooding on the Piscataquis River tributaries.

Greenville.wildlife_intro:

Village homes see raccoons, skunks and squirrels, beavers flood the woods roads and tote roads in every direction, and fishers are a real concern for outdoor cats and poultry in the woods settlements.

Remote properties need jobs done completely in one trip, and that is how our crew plans Greenville work — full inspection, full sealing, porcupine armor where the chewing history demands it, and bat exclusions scheduled around Maine law for unoccupied buildings. Raccoons forage all three shores and den in village chimneys and attics, bats summer in the older homes, and beavers work every slow stretch and side brook, flooding roads and camp lots. Monson is the last trail town before the 100-Mile Wilderness, and its buildings sit deep in woods country. Camps around Lake Hebron and the ponds stand empty for long stretches, and porcupines chew their woodwork all winter while red squirrels and bats claim the eaves and lofts in their seasons. Village homes see raccoons and skunks along the lake shore, beavers flood the pond roads and tote roads, and fishers hunt the forest that begins at every backyard.

Camp owners here often live far away, so our crew works to a simple standard: inspect everything, fix everything found, and leave the building able to sit empty safely. That means full sealing, porcupine armor on the known chew points, and bat exclusions scheduled around Maine's June and July rule for unoccupied buildings. Hiker-season businesses get the same treatment with an eye to the calendar. Call us before you close the camp or open for the season — in Monson, the woods always move back in when a building goes quiet.
